blindSummary:
This is the most protective of the large destination countries for transgender visitors. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the federal human-rights statute and the penal code's hate-crime provisions (a 2017 law); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (the authorities have neither issued nor received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; a national LGBTIQ organisation documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and two of the country's larger provinces have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of LGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets.
blindOutOfScope: Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals.
blindSourceSummaries: The national statistical agency (March 2026): police-reported hate crime in 2024 was relatively stable (4,882 incidents, +1%) after a 34% jump 2022-2023; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658; overall hate crime has more than doubled since 2018.

A national LGBTIQ organisation's UN human-rights review submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in this country - sexual orientation covered by the constitutional rights charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the international SOGI human-rights principles.

Public broadcaster (April 2016): one of the country's smallest provinces moved to make it easier for trans people to change gender on official documents - a registry-law amendment requires only a declaration of identified gender plus a doctor's letter, removing the surgery requirement; welcomed by the trans community.

National daily (June 2017): the upper house passed the 2017 gender-identity bill (67-11), prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and expression - framed as national leadership amid global backlash; contrasts with anti-LGBT violence elsewhere.

The largest province's human-rights commission policy on discrimination because of sexual orientation: the legal context, case law and legislation under the provincial human-rights code (which also covers gender identity and gender expression) - official provincial human-rights framework.
